The Ideas of Totalitarianism: What Were They Thinking!

By Leon Aron,

resident scholar and director of Russian studies at the American Enterprise Institute; and author of the upcoming " Yeltsin: A Revolutionary Life. "
Monday, February 7, 2000; Page C09

REFLECTIONS ON A RAVAGED CENTURY

By Robert Conquest

Norton. 317 pp. $26.95

" The century-wolfhound springs onto my shoulders. " One of this century's greatest poets, Osip Mandelstam, wrote this in March 1931--long before the Great Purge, the Holocaust and his death from starvation in the Gulag seven years later. Yet Robert Conquest, a lover and connoisseur of Russian poetry, is likely to agree that Mandelstam's image would make a perfect epigraph to this book on the century of " fatal ideas " in which humanity was " savaged and trampled by rogue ideologies. "

A man of many talents (he is a poet, translator, and writer of fiction, biography and criticism, as well as a world-renowned historian of Soviet Russia), Conquest belongs to the small--often besieged and sometimes vilified, but hardy--troop of giants who made the exploration of totalitarian " unfreedom " and the defense of the free world the business of their lives: the philosophers Raymond Aron, Hannah Arendt and Isaiah Berlin; and the writers George Orwell, Arthur Koestler, Albert Camus (in " L'Homme Revolte " ), Vasily Grossman (in " Life and Fate " and " Forever Flowing " ) and Alexander Solzhenitsyn. In that glorious battalion, Conquest's company is that of brilliant historians of pre-communist and Soviet Russia: Martin Malia, Richard Pipes, Leonard Schapiro and Adam Ulam. Over almost four decades, Conquest was the most indefatigable, stubborn (and, in retrospect, amazingly clairvoyant) compiler of the secret grisly record of Soviet totalitarianism.

In this book, his subject is not so much the totalitarian institutions, the technology of power or the record of the horrors (all of which he has dissected in his classics " The Great Terror " and " The Harvest of Sorrow " ) but, rather, the totalitarian " Ideas " --ideas that " claimed to transcend all problems, but were defective or delusive, devastated minds, and movements, and whole countries, and looked like plausible contenders for world supremacy. " It is the analysis of these " Ideas, " their intellectual pedigree, the secret of their appeal, their astounding resilience in the face of repeated and abject failures, and challenges they still pose to the free world, that Conquest masterfully sets forth.

This exposition is the book's scholarly and analytical heart, and the chapters on Marxism, National Socialism, the totalitarian state, the Cold War and the " Soviet morass " are superb, with the last one the best 30-page rendering of the political, social, moral and economic aspects of the Soviet experiment I have seen anywhere. Yet it is the story of the " intellectual and moral disgrace " of the " progressive " Western intelligentsia that this reader found most riveting. The record--not new in the main, but retold by Conquest with characteristic vigor and immediacy--makes for an absorbing read. In the absence of a very unlikely collective mea culpa by the accused (and with most of the main sinners dead), it is also as close as we are likely to get to a reckoning, and lessons for the future.

The gravamen of Conquest's indictment is the abdication of intellectuals' " moral duty " to know the facts and tell the truth, to speak up against the worst, most pernicious variety of " non-freedom " and to defend free societies into which they had the supreme luck to be born. The record laid out in the book prompts questions that will be pondered for as long as we care about intellectual honesty and responsibility, the inexhaustible and all-conquering human ability for self-deception and the dark, blinding power of political religions.

Taking up the leitmotifs of Berlin's and Aron's work--liberty, its vulnerabilities, strengths, sources of renewal and decay--Conquest surveys political cultures of the United States and Britain today with a trained eye and finds threats to freedom in " passionate " politics that turn competing interests into " causes " ; giant government and corporate bureaucracies; and, of course, academia, with its various " studies " and " ephemeral orthodoxies. "

For all the intellectual seriousness, even solemnity of the issues discussed, this is one of those increasingly rare and precious social science books whose value is far in excess of their summaries. Illuminated by lines from Pushkin, Dostoevsky, Chekhov, Turgenev, Babel, Pasternak, Brodsky, Auden, Yeats and Mandelstam (alongside Gibbon, Aristotle and Spencer), this volume sparkles with wit and is replete with aphorisms. One is loath to skip even a line for fear of missing a gem. (Only one chapter--on united Europe, to which Conquest is bitterly opposed--seems overlong and somewhat out of place in this book.) Like a well-aged port, Robert Conquest's book is rich, translucent and polished. It delivers its heady, high-octane content elegantly, and invigorates and satisfies, deliciously, at almost every gulp.
